passage:
Saturday afternoon, Uday looked in on his daughter Jaya three times. She was at her laptop cutting a short animation of a paper boat, headphones on, a pencil stuck in her hair. At dusk she walked out humming, hungry, and showed him the boat crossing a puddle.
Tuesday was different. She lay on her bed scrolling through clips for hours, thumb flicking, and at dinner she snapped at her brother and pushed her plate away.
On Thursday Uday, unsure whether to worry, asked only, "How do you feel after the boat, and after the clips?"
Jaya thought. "The boat, like I made something. The clips, just itchy."

qa.q: What did Jaya's animation show?
qa.a: A paper boat crossing a puddle.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling as he watched Jaya on those two days?
qa.a: He felt unsure and a little worried. He could not tell whether her long hours were absorbing or a habit, so he asked how she felt afterwards.

qa.q: Which choice by Uday on Thursday helped him learn the difference?
qa.a: He asked how she felt after each activity instead of banning either one. Her own answer showed the boat left her feeling she had made something.

qa.q: How does Jaya seem to experience the two kinds of screen time?
qa.a: The animation is rewarding and leaves her cheerful and hungry. The clips leave her restless and snappish, which she describes as itchy.

grounding: A parent cannot tell whether a teenager's long screen time is flow or capture until the aftermath shows the difference.

passage:
Come and sit, Saurabh. Your grandmother Elizabeth has a story about your uncle Danny at your age.
He would disappear into the back room for hours with a broken radio, wires everywhere. When he came out his eyes were bright and he could explain how the little coil worked. Then, that winter, he began spending afternoons at the game parlour by the bus stand. He came home grey and jumpy, answering in grunts.
From the doorway I could not tell which was which. So I stopped guessing. Afterwards I asked, "What did you learn today, and how do you feel now?"
Danny went quiet. The next week he took the radio parts to school, and the parlour slowly stopped calling him.

qa.q: Where did Danny spend his afternoons that winter?
qa.a: At the game parlour by the bus stand.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel about not being able to tell which activity was good for Danny?
qa.a: She felt uncertain and worried. She could not tell from the doorway, so she stopped guessing.

qa.q: What choice did Elizabeth make instead of forbidding either activity?
qa.a: She asked Danny afterwards what he had learned and how he felt. That let the difference show in his own answers.

qa.q: How did Danny seem to feel after the parlour compared with after the radio?
qa.a: After the radio he was bright-eyed and able to explain things. After the parlour he was grey, jumpy and answered only in grunts.

grounding: An elder recalls telling flow from screen capture by what a teenager was like afterwards.

passage:
It was exam week, and Naveen had promised himself he wouldn't hover. Still, when the clock passed eleven and Avni had been on her laptop since dinner, he stood outside her door, torn. Was this another night lost to videos? He could hear clicking, a few notes of piano, then silence, then the same notes again.
At half past eleven the power went out across the colony. Naveen braced for a slammed door.
Instead Avni came out with a torch, cheeks flushed. "Papa, listen before the battery dies." She played him forty seconds of a tune she had built, layer by layer, on a music app. "I fixed the bridge part. It took me four hours." She was grinning, wide awake, chattering about chords.
Naveen let out a breath. It was late, and there was the exam. But this didn't look like a child who had been emptied out.

qa.q: What did Avni play for Naveen when the power went out?
qa.a: Forty seconds of a tune she had built, layer by layer, on a music app.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling outside Avni's door?
qa.a: Naveen felt torn and uneasy, unsure whether she was absorbed in something good or losing another night to videos in exam week.

qa.q: What could Naveen watch for to tell flow from capture in future?
qa.a: How Avni comes out afterwards: grinning and eager to share what she made, or drained and restless.

qa.q: How did the four hours feel for Avni?
qa.a: For Avni they felt rewarding and energising; she came out flushed and grinning, proud to have fixed the bridge part.

grounding: Shows a parent unable to tell if a teenager's hours on a screen are flow or compulsion, until the energised aftermath shows it.

passage:
From the kitchen of their Bengaluru flat, Kavitha could see Siddharth on the sofa, phone held close to his face, thumb flicking upward. He had been there since four. Now it was past seven. He looked so focused she almost left him alone; last month he had spent a whole Sunday on a model aircraft with the same stillness.
When she called him for dinner, he came slowly, rubbing his eyes. He pushed rice around his plate, snapped at his sister for humming, and said he had a headache. "What were you watching?" Kavitha asked. He shrugged. "Stuff. I don't know." After dinner he picked the phone up, put it down, then picked it up again.
The aircraft Sunday had ended with him showing everyone the wings. Tonight he couldn't remember a thing.

qa.q: Since when had Siddharth been on the sofa with his phone?
qa.a: Since four; it was now past seven.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha almost leave Siddharth alone?
qa.a: Kavitha was unsure, because his stillness looked like the absorbed focus of the model-aircraft Sunday, and she didn't want to interrupt wrongly.

qa.q: What small step could Kavitha take after dinner?
qa.a: Kavitha could gently point out how drained he seems compared with the aircraft day, and suggest leaving the phone in another room for the evening.

qa.q: What is the evening like for Siddharth?
qa.a: Siddharth feels drained and restless, with a headache, snapping at his sister and unable to remember what he watched.

grounding: Shows a parent comparing a teenager's absorbed hours and finding the drained, restless aftermath of screen capture.

passage:
"Nandini, it's been five hours. Are you okay in there?"
"Mm. Almost done. One more bug."
Zainab hovered at the door. "Is this the game again?"
"No, Ammi, I'm making one. Look, the frog jumps now!"
"You haven't eaten."
"Two minutes."
Twenty minutes later Nandini came into the kitchen, stretching. "I fixed the jump. And I sort of figured out how gravity works in the code."
"How do you feel?"
Nandini thought. "Weirdly awake. Like after swimming. Not like after those Sunday games, when I feel like a wet towel."
Zainab smiled and pushed a plate across. "So that's the difference."
"What difference?"
"Never mind. Eat."
Nandini ate standing up, still talking about the frog, while Zainab listened.

qa.q: What did Nandini fix in the game?
qa.a: The jump; the frog jumps now.

qa.q: What was Zainab worried about while hovering at the door?
qa.a: Zainab was worried that five hours on the screen meant Nandini was stuck in a game again rather than doing something good.

qa.q: What question helped Zainab tell flow from capture, and why?
qa.a: "How do you feel?" Asking afterwards shows whether Nandini is energised or drained, which is where the difference shows.

qa.q: How does Nandini describe the two kinds of screen time?
qa.a: Nandini feels "weirdly awake, like after swimming" after making the game, but "like a wet towel" after the Sunday games.

grounding: Shows a parent unsure about a teenager's long screen time and finding the answer in how the teenager feels afterwards.

passage:
I'm Neelam, Ujjwal's Ma, and I've spent this year watching my fifteen-year-old son sit at his screen for hours, wondering whether to worry.
Some Saturdays he builds a small game with code. Four hours pass. When he comes out, he's bright-eyed, talking fast, showing me a jumping character he made. He eats two plates of rice and goes out to play cricket.
Other Saturdays he watches video after video. Also four hours. But when he comes out, he's grey-faced and snappy, can't say what he watched, and lies on the sofa scrolling more.
From outside, both look the same: a boy and a screen. The difference only shows after. One leaves him full. The other leaves him empty.
Now I ask, "What did you make today?" If he has an answer, I leave him be.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal sometimes build on Saturdays?
qa.a: Some Saturdays he builds a small game with code.

qa.q: What was Neelam worried about this year?
qa.a: Neelam felt worried and unsure whether Ujjwal's long hours at the screen were healthy absorption or something harmful.

qa.q: What simple check did Neelam find useful?
qa.a: Asking "What did you make today?" and noticing whether Ujjwal comes out energised or drained after screen time.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal feel after an afternoon of watching videos?
qa.a: Ujjwal seems drained and restless, grey-faced and snappy, unable to say what he watched.

grounding: A parent observing a teenager's long screen hours learns to tell flow from capture by how he seems afterwards.
